nameStory: The Black-tailed Godwit gets its distinctive name from the bold black band across its white tail, visible when the bird flies or spreads its tail feathers. The word 'godwit' comes from Old English and likely mimics the bird's call, though the exact origins are debated among bird enthusiasts.
description: The Black-tailed Godwit is a large, elegant shorebird with impossibly long legs and an equally impressive straight bill. In breeding season, these birds sport gorgeous orange-red heads, necks, and chests that make them stand out among other shorebirds. During winter and migration, they wear more subdued gray-brown plumage, but their distinctive black and white wing pattern remains constant. These are substantial birds, much larger than most sandpipers you'd encounter.

idTips.label: Black tail band
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive black band across the white tail, most visible in flight or when the bird stretches - this is like the bird's signature stripe

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: In flight, notice the bold white wingbar that contrasts sharply with darker wing feathers, creating a striking pattern that flashes as they fly

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: The long, straight bill is perfectly suited for probing mud - unlike the slightly upturned bills of some relatives, this one is poker-straight

idTips.label: Breeding colors
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, the orange-red head, neck, and chest are unmistakable - like the bird dipped its front half in rusty paint

idTips.label: Leg length
idTips.description: The exceptionally long legs extend well beyond the tail in flight, making the bird look almost comically stretched out

habitat: In New England, you'd be extraordinarily lucky to spot one of these European visitors - there's only been one confirmed sighting! If one does show up, look for it in coastal mudflats, salt marshes, or shallow freshwater wetlands where it can wade and probe for food. Unlike some shorebirds that prefer strictly marine environments, Black-tailed Godwits often favor freshwater areas and might turn up at inland ponds or flooded fields.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration time when a vagrant might appear, displaying the spectacular orange-red breeding plumage on head, neck, and chest.
seasonality.summer: Extremely unlikely to see one as they'd be on breeding grounds in Europe and Asia, though breeding plumage would still be visible if one appeared.
seasonality.fall: Another potential window for vagrant sightings, though birds would be molting into duller winter plumage with gray-brown replacing the bright orange-red.
seasonality.winter: Very unlikely season for sightings, but any bird present would show subdued gray-brown coloring while retaining the diagnostic tail and wing patterns.

funFact: The Black-tailed Godwit is the national bird of the Netherlands, where it's so beloved that Dutch conservationists have created special 'godwit-friendly' farming practices to help protect their wetland breeding areas - imagine having agricultural policies designed around a single bird species!
confusionNotes: In New England, you're most likely to confuse this ultra-rare visitor with the more common Hudsonian Godwit. Remember: Black-tailed has a bold white wingbar (Hudsonian's is less distinct) and the tail pattern is reversed - Black-tailed shows black on white, while Hudsonian shows white on black. Think 'Black-tailed = black stripe on white tail.'
contextualKnowledge: This bird represents the ultimate 'vagrant' experience for New England birders - a species so far from its normal range that seeing one here would be a once-in-a-lifetime event. The single New England record makes this bird more of a 'what to dream about' than a realistic field identification challenge for most nature explorers.
compareHints: Among the godwits, Black-tailed is the only one with that distinctive white wingbar and the black-on-white tail pattern. Compared to the Hudsonian Godwit you might actually see in New England, Black-tailed is slightly larger with a straighter bill, and it strongly prefers freshwater habitats over purely coastal environments. The Marbled Godwit is much larger with a distinctly upturned bill and completely different coloring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the Marbled Godwit (the other godwit regularly seen in New England), Hudsonian Godwits are smaller with a straighter bill and completely different wing pattern in flight.
Among the godwits, Marbled Godwits are the largest and show the most consistent warm brown coloration throughout the year.
Compared to the Hudsonian Godwit (the most similar species), bar-tailed godwits have that distinctive upturned bill and lack the bold white wing patches.
